source_text: Possit in isto capitulo etiam de militia definitum uideri, quae inter dignitatem et potestatem est. at nunc de isto quaeritur, an fidelis ad militiam conuerti possit et an militia ad fidem admitti, etiam caligata uel inferior quaeque, cui non sit necessitas immolationum uel capitalium iudiciorum. non conuenit sacramento diuino et humano, signo Christi et signo diaboli, castris lucis et castris tenebrarum; non potest una anima duobus deberi, deo et Caesari. et virgam portavit Moyses, fibulam et Aaron, cingitur loro et Iohannes, agmen agit et Iesus Naue, bellauit et populus, si placet ludere. quomodo autem bellabit, immo quomodo etiam in pace militabit sine gladio, quem dominus abstulit? nam etsi adierant milites ad Iohannem et formam obseruationis acceperant, si etiam centurio crediderat, omnem postea militem dominus in Petro exarmando discinxit. nullus habitus licitus est apud nos illicito actui adscriptus.
thought_title: Military service cannot be joined with the faith
orientation: Tertullian has just said that the only remedy for the trouble of birth and property is to be fortunate in heaven, not as a magistrate on earth; now he turns to the question of military service.
pass_a_gloss: It could in this chapter also about military service [to] have been defined [as] seen, which is between dignity and power. But now about this it is asked, whether a believer to military service [to] be converted can, and whether military service to the faith [to] be admitted, even [the] booted [service] or [the] lower [service] of whatever kind, to which there is not [a] necessity of sacrifices or of capital judgments. [It] does not agree [with] [the] sacred commitment divine and human, [with] [the] sign of Christ and [the] sign of [the] devil, [with] [the] camp of light and [the] camp of darkness; [it] cannot [that] one soul to two [masters] be owed, to God and to Caesar. And [a] rod carried Moses, [a] buckle also Aaron, [he] is girded with [a] leather strap also John, [a] battle line leads also Joshua, [it] waged war also [the] people, if [it] pleases [you] to play. But how will [he] wage war, rather how also in peace will [he] serve as [a] soldier without [a] sword, which [the] Lord took away? For even if [they] had come [as] soldiers to John and [a] form of observance had received, if also [the] centurion had believed, every afterwards soldier [the] Lord in Peter [by] disarming unbuckled. No dress is permitted among us [to] [an] unlawful act assigned.

choices.english: the divine sacred commitment and the human one
choices.why: Keeps the glossary term 'sacred commitment' for sacramentum and preserves the parallel between the two oaths.
rejected: the divine oath and the human oath

choices.english: the booted service or any lower kind
choices.why: Caligata refers to the common soldier's boot, marking the lowest rank; 'lower kind' keeps the sense of any service below that.

choices.term: non potest una anima duobus deberi, deo et Caesari
choices.english: one soul cannot be owed to two masters, to God and to Caesar
choices.why: Deberi means 'to be owed' as a debt of allegiance; 'two masters' makes the echo of the Lord's saying clear.
rejected: one soul cannot serve two, God and Caesar
one soul cannot be due to two

choices.term: omnem postea militem dominus in Petro exarmando discinxit
choices.english: the Lord afterwards unbuckled every soldier by disarming Peter
choices.why: Discinxit means 'unbuckled' or 'ungirded,' matching the military image of the belt; 'by disarming Peter' keeps the instrumental force of exarmando.
rejected: the Lord stripped every soldier by disarming Peter
the Lord ungirded every soldier in Peter

choices.term: nullus habitus licitus est apud nos illicito actui adscriptus
choices.english: No dress is permitted among us that is assigned to an unlawful act
choices.why: Habitus means the distinctive dress or uniform; 'assigned to' keeps adscriptus as a legal term of attachment.
rejected: No clothing is lawful among us assigned to an unlawful act
No uniform is allowed among us for an unlawful act

bible_refs.note: Render to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's; Tertullian's 'one soul cannot be owed to two masters, to God and to Caesar' echoes this saying.
Put your sword back in its place; the Lord's taking away of the sword in Peter refers to this.
Soldiers came to John and received a form of observance; this refers to the Baptist's answer to the soldiers.

pass_b_english: This chapter might also settle the question of military service, which stands between rank and power. But the question now is whether a believer can turn to military service, and whether the military can be admitted to the faith—even the booted service or any lower kind, where there is no necessity of sacrifices or capital judgments. The divine sacred commitment and the human one do not agree, nor the sign of Christ and the sign of the devil, nor the camp of light and the camp of darkness. One soul cannot be owed to two masters, to God and to Caesar (Matthew 22:21). Moses carried a rod, Aaron a buckle, John is girded with a strap, Joshua led a battle line, and the people waged war—if you want to play games. But how will he wage war, indeed how will he even serve in peace without a sword, which the Lord took away? For even if soldiers had come to John and received a form of observance, and even if a centurion had believed, the Lord afterwards unbuckled every soldier by disarming Peter (Matthew 26:52). No dress is permitted among us that is assigned to an unlawful act.

last_rejected.quote: the Lord afterwards unbuckled every soldier by disarming Peter
last_rejected.source_quote: omnem postea militem dominus in Petro exarmando discinxit
last_rejected.why: Latin 'discinxit' means 'cut off' or 'separated', not 'unbuckled'; the action is removal from service, not unbuckling.
last_rejected.fix: the Lord, by disarming Peter, cut off every soldier
last_rejected.ruling: 'discinxit' literally means ungirded/unbuckled; metaphorically removes from service. Translation captures both literal and figurative sense adequately.
